title: Riding a coal car under the coal to Cincinnati
summary: They hoboed on a flat car buried in coal through a mile tunnel, then shared a boxcar fire and hobo meals in Cincinnati.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Tell me about the journey -- when you actually hoboed. What was jumping a freight train like? Did you ever do this again, or was this the only time...?
Oh, no. That was the first and last time.
What was the journey like? What happened?

Oh, we went on down there and caught one of those big freight trains comin' out of Florida or Alabama or somewhere, South Carolina... Yeah, Chesapeake. Chesapeake Bay. It was of them big-big, long trains, about 300 coaches on it, and it was running! We went down into and clean into the mountains, and it got to slow up... One of them great big engines. And it slowed up and it was running at about 15-20 miles an hour, you know. And it had 32 people on it, just on the engine. And we all had to wrap(?) that baby... So the boys all got...we all got on the same side -- on the right-hand side, I think...
And the train was going 15 miles an hour?
Yeah, going about 15 miles an hour. They said,
Buster Smith - 211

"Every man get on there and you grab a coach by yourself." Said, "Grab on the front of the coach. Don't grab the back of the coach. When the coach get there, grab the front of it, so if you miss that piece up there and the train throw you loose, you hit against the coach and it will knock you off the track, but if you catch on the back end of it you'll liable to fall in between there and the coach right behind that will run over you."
Which one of you had done this before? Who knew this?
Oh, I don't know. I think Ernie Williams and Theodore Ross, they'd been doing that.
Oh really?
Yes.
When you got on the coach, was it like something you could get inside, or was it a flat car?
No, we found a flat car. We mostly got on the flat car...
So you were open to the air.
Yeah.
Weren't you freezing cold?
No, we got on (?) and there coal on it, and we jumped down and got under that coal.
Under the coal.
Yeah, got down under that coal. Wasn't nothin' sticking out but your head!
Buster Smith - 212
You're kidding!
Yes.
You rode in a flat car full of coal...
Yeah.
...with no roof.
No.
And you were buried up to your neck in coal.

Yes! Heh...! And we had to come through a tunnel I guess about... Oh, we got on there and we didn't even go more than I guess about two blocks, and it was going through a tunnel. And that tunnel was a mile long. Yeah. Now, I said, "It's going through the tunnel, and everybody get on now and get situated, because going through that tunnel you won't be able to see anything. It's black-dark going through there. I says, "Don't get on one of them high cars. You have to get on one of them flat cars, because that tunnel's liable to be..."
Just inches above.
Yeah, just inches above that car, so that you had all that (?).
And there was no possibility of getting inside a boxcar?
No. Those were all locked. You couldn't get in there, because the train was going fast and you didn't have nothin' to catch on to, to hold on to get into it.
How long did the journey take?
Buster Smith - 213
Oh, overnight.
Oh, just one night.
Yeah. We got on it right after dark, and the next day, about 10 or 11 o'clock, we was in Cincinnati, Ohio.
You got off in Cincinnati or St. Louis.

It stopped two or three different places. When daylight came, we run into some White boys, and they was in one of those big boxcars that was open. They done shoved the door open, there wasn't nothin' in there, and they was all sittin' in there, so we made a big fire. It was kind of cold.
So you lit a fire in the boxcar.
Yeah.
You went inside with them?
Yeah. We got a big piece of tin and laid it down there so we wouldn't burn a hole in it. 21 of us was in there.
You must have been filthy after you'd been covered up with coal.
Yeah. I had a white suit, and then ...(?)... and then it was blacker than them shoes I've got on now.
Were you in the coal to keep warm?
Yeah. Man, you'll freeze to death comin' through them mountains. Cold! Froze... Yeah, through the mountains.
You must have been really desperate.
Yeah. We made it all right. We went up there to
Buster Smith - 214

Cincinnati and we stayed around there a day. Down there in the hobo city we ran up on some more guys traveling, some goin' to New York... Just a whole bunch of them down there. Hoboes. We sit around there and we didn't have buy nothing to eat. Them White boys went out there and got us plenty to eat. Got steaks, brought them back. They already cooked great big pieces of ham, all the bacon you wanted...
Did they give you any?
Yeah. Give it to us. They said, 'Now, don't you'all go out through there. Some of them people will jump on you. So we'll go get you something to eat.' Man, they was good to us.
